title: Loops
summary: A loop is a jump backwards. Counting loops often count down to zero with dec and jnz, since dec sets the zero flag for free. A while loop tests at the top and a do-while at the bottom; compilers prefer the bottom test with one check in front. Reading until read_int reports the end of the input makes a loop over all the input.
markdown:
## A jump backwards

```nasm
        global  _start
        section .text
_start:
        mov     ebx, 1                  ; i = 1
.loop:
        mov     edi, ebx
        call    print_int
        call    print_newline
        inc     ebx                     ; i++
        cmp     ebx, 5
        jle     .loop                   ; while i <= 5, go round again
        mov     eax, 60
        xor     edi, edi
        syscall
```

The counter lives in `rbx` because `print_int` may change `rcx`, `rdx`, `rsi` and `rdi`.

## Counting down to zero

`dec` sets ZF when it reaches zero, so a loop that counts down needs no `cmp`:

```demo-asm
title: Add up 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1
init: ecx=5
    xor eax, eax
top:
    add eax, ecx
    dec ecx
    jnz top
    ret
```

That is the classic assembly loop. (x86 even has a `loop` instruction that decrements `rcx` and jumps, but on modern processors it is slower than `dec` + `jnz`, so compilers never use it.)

## while and do-while

A **do-while** tests at the bottom, so the body always runs at least once:

```nasm-norun
.body:
        ; ...
        cmp     ...
        jcc     .body
```

A **while** loop must test first, in case it should run zero times. The straightforward version tests at the top and jumps back from the bottom:

```nasm-norun
.test:
        cmp     ...
        jcc     .end            ; the opposite condition: leave the loop
        ; ... body ...
        jmp     .test
.end:
```

That is two jumps per round. Compilers turn it into a single test in front plus a do-while, called a **rotated** loop, which takes one jump per round:

```nasm-norun
        cmp     ...
        jcc     .end            ; skip the loop entirely if it should not run
.body:
        ; ... body ...
        cmp     ...
        jcc     .body           ; one jump per round
.end:
```

## Reading until the end of the input

`read_int` returns `rdx = 0` when there are no more numbers. Testing it after each call makes a loop over the whole input:

```nasm
        global  _start
        section .data
s_count: db     " numbers, total ", 0

        section .text
_start:
        xor     ebx, ebx                ; total
        xor     r12d, r12d              ; count
.next:
        call    read_int
        test    rdx, rdx
        jz      .done                   ; no more numbers
        add     rbx, rax
        inc     r12
        jmp     .next
.done:
        mov     rdi, r12
        call    print_int
        lea     rdi, [rel s_count]
        call    print_str
        mov     rdi, rbx
        call    print_int
        call    print_newline
        mov     eax, 60
        xor     edi, edi
        syscall
```

Try it with several numbers on several lines.

## Loops inside loops

Keep each counter in its own register that survives the calls inside (here `r12` and `r13`):

```nasm
        global  _start
        section .text
_start:
        mov     r12d, 1                 ; row
.row:
        mov     r13d, 1                 ; column
.col:
        mov     edi, '*'
        call    print_char
        inc     r13d
        cmp     r13d, r12d
        jle     .col                    ; columns 1..row
        call    print_newline
        inc     r12d
        cmp     r12d, 4
        jle     .row
        mov     eax, 60
        xor     edi, edi
        syscall
```

## Check yourself
```quiz
? Why does dec ecx followed by jnz top work without a cmp?
- jnz compares ecx with 0 itself
- dec jumps automatically
+ dec sets the zero flag when ecx reaches 0
> Arithmetic sets the flags as a side effect.

? Which loop always runs its body at least once?
- One that tests at the top (while)
- Neither
+ One that tests at the bottom (do-while)
> A while loop may run zero times.

? Why keep a loop counter in rbx or r12 to r15 when the loop calls print_int?
- Only those registers can count
- Those registers are faster than the others
+ Calls may change rcx, but not rbx or r12 to r15
> By the calling convention, routines may change rcx, rdx, rsi and rdi, but must keep rbx and r12 to r15.

? How does a loop over all the input know when to stop?
- read_int returns -1 in rax
+ read_int returns rdx = 0 at the end
- The program crashes at the end
> Test rdx after each call; -1 is a number the input could really contain.
```
